summary: Esther's prayer — the queen lays aside her royal robes, covers her head with ashes, tears her hair, and fasts. Then she speaks to God with shocking honesty: she abhors the sign of her glory on her head, 'as a menstruous rag'; she never ate at Aman's table; since she came to this house she has rejoiced in nothing 'but in thee, O Lord, the God of Abraham.' She asks for one thing: 'a well ordered speech in my mouth in the presence of the lion.'
whyItMatters: The Hebrew Esther is a woman of perfect composure who never prays. The Greek Esther is a terrified young woman who prays magnificently — and the addition gives the book its soul. Her prayer holds together two things we usually separate: total honesty about her situation, and total trust in the only helper she has.

keyVerses.text: O my Lord, who alone art our king, help me a desolate woman, and who have no other helper but thee.
keyVerses.why: The queen of the empire calls herself desolate — the prayer's posture in one line.

keyVerses.text: Give me a well ordered speech in my mouth in the presence of the lion, and turn his heart to the hatred of our enemy.
keyVerses.why: She asks not for rescue but for words — rhetoric as a gift of God. The 'lion' is the king; the request is precision under pressure.

keyVerses.text: Thou knowest my necessity, that I abominate the sign of my pride and glory, which is upon my head in the days of my public appearance, and detest it as a menstruous rag.
keyVerses.why: The most startling line in the additions — the crown she must wear is, to her, uncleanness. The prayer refuses to let the reader envy the palace.

keyVerses.text: O God, who art mighty above all, hear the voice of them, that have no other hope, and deliver us from the hand of the wicked, and deliver me from my fear.
keyVerses.why: She prays with her people, not above them — and the last deliverance she names is from her own fear.

questions.question: Why does Esther pray so differently from the Hebrew book?
questions.answer: In the Hebrew text Esther never prays — she acts, brilliantly, and God is never named. The Greek additions give her an interior life: fear, fasting, and this prayer. The two versions are almost two different theologies of the same events — hidden providence versus open dependence — and the church kept both.

questions.question: Why ashes, dung, and torn hair?
questions.answer: The mourning rites of her people, taken to the extreme — the queen deliberately unqueens herself before approaching the king. The outward signs match the prayer's inner claim: the crown is 'a menstruous rag' to her. She goes to the lion as a beggar, not a rival beauty.

questions.question: Is her complaint about her marriage fair?
questions.answer: The prayer says she 'abhor[s] the bed of the uncircumcised' (14:15) and has never rejoiced since she was taken (14:18). It is the voice of a woman in a forced marriage to a pagan king — a situation the Hebrew book never lets her comment on. The addition lets her grieve it without making her disobedient: she works within it, and prays through it.

questions.question: Why does she confess 'we have worshipped their gods'?
questions.answer: She includes herself in the nation's sin — the same solidarity Nehemiah shows. 'Thou art just, O Lord' (14:7) concedes that the danger is deserved; only then does she ask for deliverance. The prayer's logic runs: justice acknowledged, mercy requested, glory of God's name at stake (14:9).

questions.question: What does 'give not thy sceptre to them that are not' mean?
questions.answer: Literally, 'to those who are nothing' — do not let being itself pass to non-beings, the idols and their servants. It is a striking way to call idolatry nihilistic: the enemy worships what does not exist, and if they win, the world belongs to nothing.

glossary.def: Haman, whose table Esther says she never shared.
The Persian king — the lion was a royal symbol; approaching unsummoned carried the death penalty.
The king's rod; Esther's later touch of it (chapter 15) marks acceptance of her approach.
